sections.summary: The speaker says the issue threatens individual well-being and social defence, and supports the Bill strengthening protection against race and religion discrimination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Left unaddressed, it threatens not only individual well-being but also the trust and respect that underpin our social defence, a critical pillar of our Total Defence strategy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: I therefore stand in support of the Bill which strengthens protection against discrimination based on race and religion.

sections.label: Claims-based approach questioned
sections.summary: The speaker says a claims-based approach may not address the sensitivities involved or achieve harmonious, diverse and productive workplaces.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: A claims-based approach may not be adequate to grapple with the sensitivities of the issues involved, beyond the individuals affected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Resolving issues through discrimination claims under the legislation will not lead to the goal of achieving harmonious, diverse and productive workplaces to power Singapore’s economy.

sections.label: Tudung for Muslim healthcare staff
sections.summary: From 2021, Muslim public healthcare staff including nurses could wear a tudung at work if they chose to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: From 2021, Muslim staff working in the public healthcare sector including nurses were allowed to wear a tudung or headscarf at work if they chose to do so.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In a multi-racial, religious Singapore, we will need to work through these issues together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: But let us do so sensitively and in a spirit of mutual understanding, rather than through a legal claims process. : Mr Speaker, Sir, to conclude, the Workplace Fairness Bill is a significant step forward, but it is only the beginning.

sections.label: Malay/Muslim community issues
sections.summary: The Member says interactions with some in the Malay/Muslim community showed these issues need addressing, best through the Workplace Fairness Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
sentences.text: I have got this information through my interactions with some in the Malay/Muslim community, that these issues need to be addressed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
sentences.text: And I guess, one of the best ways to address it is through this Workplace Fairness Bill.

sections.label: Minister asked to add clarity
sections.summary: The Speaker asks Minister Tan See Leng to add clarity, after the Member sought understanding from MP Mr Faisal Manap.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Minister Tan See Leng, do you want to add some clarity to this?

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: I did not want to venture into this discussion, but for the purpose of my wrapping-up speech later, I just needed to understand from the Member of Parliament, Mr Faisal Manap.

sections.label: Clarification on gender equality and Friday prayers
sections.summary: The Member says Friday prayers are obligatory only on male Muslims and seeks confirmation that his two cited scenarios fall under the legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: On his seeking of clarification regarding the gender equality, if I can put it that way, basically, as what I have quoted yesterday, even the former Member of Parliament, Mr Zainal Sapari, and I think most Muslims know, the Friday prayers are only obligatory upon the male Muslims, not for females.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: And my clarification yesterday was pertaining to the two scenarios to get an affirmation and certainty from the Minister that the two scenarios have been happening for so many years, and are even reflected in the Suara Musyawarah, which is the Singapore Conversations equivalent, and even the issue about Friday prayers being highlighted on social media by Assistant Secretary-General, Mr Zainal Sapari.

sentences.speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
sentences.text: So, I just want to have a confirmation and certainty that the two scenarios that I cited yesterday can come under the legislation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: After hesitation for several years, the Government has heeded calls from several quarters, including from the Workers’ Party (WP), to go beyond Tripartite Guidelines and to legislate against discrimination in the workplace.

sections.label: Workplace Fairness Bill tabled in two parts
sections.summary: The Minister said the Bill would be tabled that month, in two parts, with provisions effective in 2026 or 2027.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Minister replied then that the Workforce Fairness Bill would be tabled in Parliament that month.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: We understand that the legislation is being tabled in two parts, the first part now and with a second part on employment claims, to be tabled later this year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government has announced that the provisions of both parts would be effective in 2026 or 2027, that is, possibly two years from now.

sections.label: Eleven protected characteristics listed
sections.summary: The Bill lists 11 protected characteristics that employers should not use to discriminate against jobseekers or employees.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Bill lists 11 protected characteristics, meaning that employers should not use those characteristics to discriminate against jobseekers or employees.

sections.label: Protected characteristics and language clause
sections.summary: The speaker warns that asking about protected characteristics lets employers disguise decisions, and notes clause 20 on language ability.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If questions about the protected characteristics continue to be asked, it opens the door for employers to make decisions based on those characteristics, but to disguise the real reason in more kosher language to avoid complaints and investigations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Such a loophole should be avoided where possible, as this would render the protection toothless.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I look forward to the Ministry’s clarifications on the three points I have raised concerning timing of implementation, employers who disguise employment as contracts for service and on what is permissible during the hiring process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Clause 20 goes on to clarify that the ability to "read, speak, write or understand a language" is not considered necessary for the performance of a job, just because other employees happen to regularly communicate in that language.

sections.label: Definition excludes gender identity
sections.summary: The definition covers biological characteristics from birth and after sex re-assignment, but leaves out gender identity and sexual orientation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The definition includes biological characteristics from birth and after the completion of sex re-assignment procedures.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: What it clearly leaves out is discrimination on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation.

sections.label: Dismissal over spouse's race
sections.summary: The explanatory note on clause 17 states that dismissing someone because of their husband's race is not discrimination under the proposed law.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: At the explanatory note on clause 17, there is a statement there that when an employer dismisses someone on the ground of the race of that person’s husband, this will not be considered as discrimination under the new proposed law.

sections.label: LGBTQ+ workplace rights assurance
sections.summary: The speaker seeks assurance that LGBTQ+ workplace rights will be protected, noting clause 8 characteristics cover 95% of complaints.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, I hope the Minister takes the opportunity during this debate to assure the LGBTQ+ community that their rights in the workplace will be protected, regardless of the wording in clause 10(2) of this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I note from a Straits Times article in November 2024 that the protected characteristics set out in clause 8 of the Bill account for 95% of workplace discrimination complaints which have been made to MOM and the TAFEP.

sections.label: Survey on workplace discrimination
sections.summary: A survey of around 700 respondents found almost one third experienced discrimination over sexual orientation or gender identity, and close to half reported harassment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to the report, which was based on a survey of around 700 respondents, almost one third had experienced at least one form of discrimination in the workplace due to their sexual orientation or gender identity.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Close to half of the people surveyed reported some form of harassment at the workplace.

sections.label: Review of clause 4(1) exemption
sections.summary: MOM's factsheet states tripartite partners will review the clause 4(1) exemption in five years' time.

sentences.speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: MOM has indicated in its factsheet on the proposed Bill that tripartite partners will review the exemption set out at clause 4(1) of the Bill in five years’ time.

sections.label: Mental health productivity losses
sections.summary: Duke-NUS and Institute of Mental Health research estimates anxiety and depression cost Singapore about 2.9% of GDP annually, or S$16 billion in productivity losses.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Research by Duke-NUS Medical School and the Institute of Mental Health estimates that anxiety and depression alone cost Singapore’s economy approximately 2.9% of gross domestic product annually, translating to a staggering S$16 billion in productivity losses.

sections.label: Bill protects mental health status
sections.summary: The Bill makes mental health a protected characteristic, bars adverse employment decisions based on it, and requires grievance processes.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The Bill addresses these gaps by recognising mental health conditions as a protected characteristic.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Employers are prohibited from making adverse decisions based on an employee’s mental health status, whether during hiring, promotions or dismissals.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: It requires that grievance processes be established to ensure employees can report discrimination without fear of retaliation.

sections.label: Mental health as national priority
sections.summary: The Government affirmed mental health as a national priority, and the Bill's inclusion of mental health translates that commitment into workplace policies.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Last year, during the Motion on mental health, the Government affirmed that mental health is a national priority.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Therefore, the inclusion of mental health in this Bill underscores that commitment, translating our national vision into actionable policies that directly impact the workplace and beyond.

sections.label: Workplace Fairness Bill discussions
sections.summary: Discussions featured the Workplace Fairness Bill as a key legislative step aligning with a shared vision of a healthier, more inclusive workplace.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: During our discussions, the Workplace Fairness Bill featured prominently as a key legislative step that aligns with our shared vision of creating a healthier, more inclusive workplace.

sections.label: Commitment to fairness and inclusivity
sections.summary: Standing against discrimination and upholding mental health reaffirms commitment to fairness, dignity and inclusivity, signalling discrimination has no place in workplaces.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: By standing against discrimination and upholding mental health as a national priority, we reaffirm our commitment to fairness, dignity and inclusivity.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Together, let us take this important step towards a society where no one feels excluded or undervalued due to their mental health challenges.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: It sends a clear message: mental health matters and discrimination has no place in our society, and especially in our workplaces.

sections.label: Clarity on Bill implementation
sections.summary: The speaker calls the Bill a sound first step and seeks clarity on how it would be implemented to counter discrimination in traditional and new workspaces.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While I acknowledge the Bill as a sound first step in the right direction, I seek clarity on how the Bill would be implemented to counter facets of discrimination in traditional and new workspaces.

sections.label: Platform workers under Platform Workers Act
sections.summary: Over 70,000 regular platform workers are protected under the Platform Workers Act effective 1 January 2025.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the context of new workspaces, over 70,000 individuals are regular platform workers and are now protected under the Platform Workers Act that has taken effect from 1 January 2025.

sections.label: Expanding Bill to platform workspace
sections.summary: The question asks if the Ministry will expand the Bill to cover platform workers facing algorithmic discrimination.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Could the Ministry consider expanding the Bill to cover the platform workspace and to provide protection to platform workers impacted by such algorithmic discrimination?

sections.label: Mandating AI Verify for platforms
sections.summary: The question asks if the Ministry will mandate platform operators to apply AI Verify and address flagged gaps.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given the push for fairer workplaces, would the Ministry consider mandating platform operators to apply AI Verify to their platform algorithms and for operators to address gaps flagged out by AI Verify?

sections.label: Discriminatory job advertising on social media
sections.summary: The question asks what measures the Ministry plans with social media platforms to prevent discriminatory job advertising under clause 19.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In respect of clause 19 of the Bill on advertising, what are measures that the Ministry plans to undertake with social media platforms to prevent employers from exploiting social media to engage in discriminatory job advertising?

sections.label: Company readiness and stakeholder support
sections.summary: The question asks the Ministry's assessment of company readiness to implement the Bill in 2026 and plans to work with stakeholders.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Despite such myths being baseless and in fact, unlawful given that it is an offence under the Industrial Relations Act to induce persons not to join trade unions or platform work associations, it remains an uphill task for the union leaders and I to debunk these myths.

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, could the Minister share the Ministry's assessment of the level of readiness of companies to implement the Bill in 2026 and if the Bill is passed?

sentences.speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Given the scale of implementation of the Bill, how does the Government plan to work with stakeholders to level up managers and human resource practitioners by 2026?

sections.label: Survey on discrimination rates
sections.summary: The survey showed about 55% of respondents experienced discrimination, with PwDs at 78% versus 50% for others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The results showed approximately 55% of respondents had experienced at least one form of discrimination in the preceding five years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: For disability-based discrimination, the survey showed that PwDs experienced discrimination at a significantly higher rate of 78%, compared to persons without disabilities who have experienced discrimination of 50%.

sections.label: Employer awareness of accommodation funding
sections.summary: The question asks how the Ministry would boost employer awareness and use of three funds covering reasonable accommodation costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: How would the Ministry boost awareness and utilisation of the Open Door Programme, Assistive Technology Fund and the Accessibility Fund by employers to fund the costs of reasonable accommodation?

sections.label: UNCRPD ratification and discrimination legislation
sections.summary: Singapore ratified the UNCRPD in 2013 and joined a Constructive Dialogue in 2022, and the speaker urges legislating against indirect discrimination and denial of reasonable accommodation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singapore ratified the United Nations Conventions on the Rights of People with Disabilities (UNCRPD) in 2013 and participated in the Constructive Dialogue with the UNCRPD Committee in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It would be timely for our Government to set a timeline and work towards legislating the prohibition of indirect discrimination and denial of reasonable accommodation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Doing so will help us move closer to achieving the Enabling MasterPlan 2030's goal of 40% PwD employment rate and upholding the UNCRPD principles.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Singapore has reached a commendable milestone in introducing the Workplace Fairness Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Our PwDs and persons with other conditions would be heartened that the Government has heard their concerns and taken the first steps to improve their employment opportunities and work environment.

sections.label: Provision applying to employers with 25 employees
sections.summary: The provision applies to employers with 25 or more employees and acknowledges SMEs often lack resources for extensive frameworks.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For example, by applying its provision to employers with 25 or more employees and acknowledges that SMEs often lack the resources to implement extensive frameworks.

sections.label: Annual accommodation costs for smaller firms
sections.summary: For smaller firms these costs can range from $5,000 to $10,000 annually, significant sums for businesses facing economic pressures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For smaller firms, these costs can range from $5,000 to $10,000 annually – significant sums for businesses already facing economic pressures.

sections.label: Fair consideration for local candidates
sections.summary: Section 26 requires employers to demonstrate fair consideration for local candidates before hiring foreign talent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Third, section 26 requires employers to demonstrate fair consideration for local candidates before hiring foreign talent.

sections.label: Frivolous complaints and SME policy fatigue
sections.summary: An underperforming employee could file a frivolous discrimination complaint to avoid dismissal, and many SMEs express concerns over policy fatigue amid multiple regulatory requirements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For instance, an underperforming employee facing dismissal could file a frivolous discrimination complaint to avoid termination, even if the action was based on legitimate reason like poor performance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Such cases could increase administrative burdens on businesses and undermine team morale. : Finally, many SMEs express concerns over "policy fatigue", particularly as they are already navigating multiple regulatory requirements.

sections.label: Tiered compliance by business size
sections.summary: A tiered compliance framework would set obligations by business size, with large firms complying in one year and SMEs having lighter requirements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Fourth, a tiered compliance framework can be adopted that differentiates obligations based on business size.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Large corporations with 250 or more employees should achieve full compliance within one year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Medium-sized firms could have up to three years to adjust, while SMEs with fewer than 25 employees could fulfil lighter but meaningful requirements.

sections.label: Exemptions for manufacturing foreign talent
sections.summary: Sectors critical to long-term goals, such as manufacturing, could get targeted exemptions or expedited processes for hiring foreign talent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Sectors critical to our long-term goals, such as manufacturing, which plays a key role in the Manufacturing 2030 ambitions, could benefit from targeted exemptions or expedited processes for hiring foreign talent.

sections.label: Support for workplace discrimination Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill, which makes it an offence to discriminate based on characteristics such as nationality, sex, marital status and disability, with carve-outs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While I have outlined some concerns and recommendations, I extend my strong support for this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This Bill gives the MOM express powers to take action against discrimination in the workplace.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: And I am grateful to the Minister and the team at MOM that has had the openness of mind to move ahead with this change.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This Bill now makes it an offence to discriminate against employees based on characteristics such as nationality, sex, marital status, pregnancy, caregiving responsibilities, language ability, disability and mental health.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: There are important carve-outs, of course, including genuine job requirements, referring citizens and PRs over foreigners, and in relation to age, having minimum age requirements.

sections.label: Personal remedy against employers
sections.summary: The speaker supports giving victims a personal remedy against employers, which the Minister's speech indicated is the intention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: One point I had also made in this House in my speech in September 2020 was that anti-discrimination legislation should ideally also give the victim a personal remedy against the employer, rather than just a punishment for the employer by the state.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I understand from the Minister's introductory speech that this is exactly the intention – and I support this as well, and look forward to the next Bill on this topic.

sections.label: Age discrimination complaint statistics
sections.summary: From 2018 to 2022, age discrimination was the second largest complaint category to TAFEP and MOM, nearly a quarter of all complaints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: From 2018 to 2022, complaints to TAFEP and MOM show that age discrimination is the second largest category, making up nearly a quarter of all complaints.

sections.label: Protections for seniors at work
sections.summary: The law targets direct discrimination, focuses on companies with over 25 employees for five years, and protects seniors' age and caregiving responsibilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: It not only targets direct discrimination but also sets the stage for a workplace culture that values inclusion and fairness.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: It focuses on clear, enforceable actions: (a) protecting seniors against direct discrimination; (b) targeting companies with more than 25 employees for the next five years; and (c) prioritising mediation through TADM to resolve disputes constructively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: It recognises the realities seniors face: (a) age is now a protected characteristic; (b) hiring practices that exclude seniors are directly addressed; and (c) caregiving responsibilities of seniors is also a protected characteristic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: This law supports employers to hire seniors above 55 when candidates are equally qualified, ensuring that experience and maturity are not overlooked.

sections.label: Workplace fairness Bill and Singapore
sections.summary: The speaker says the Bill balances workplace fairness practically, giving Singaporeans stability and keeping Singapore open amid global upheaval and high costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: I am heartened that the practical approach to fight ageism extends to most forms of discrimination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: We are staring at a period of significant upheaval – changing geopolitics, trade-flow, global taxation, technology innovation are reshaping employment everywhere.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: Singapore is not be immune from these upheavals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: Singapore has, frankly, become a high-cost location, with many employers are struggling to adapt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
sentences.text: Therefore, by having a very good balance, by strengthening workplace fairness in a practical manner, this Bill provides the stability and the fairness that Singaporeans need to thrive and for Singapore to stay open and successful.

sections.label: Women's workplace discrimination reports to PPIS
sections.summary: Women told PPIS they are passed over for promotion in childbearing years, assumed less committed, face career interruptions and gender pay gaps.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For instance, some women reported to PPIS that they are often passed over for promotion during their childbearing years, regardless of their intentions to start a family; they are frequently assumed to be less committed to their careers if they have caregiving responsibilities; they are far more likely to face interruptions in their career trajectory due to family obligations; and society and culture still assumes that there are certain roles that women are better and worse at, or should and should not do. : Women also reported to PPIS that discriminatory hiring and workplace practices are prevalent, especially in male-dominated sectors, with many women reporting a gender pay gap and gender-biased promotions.

sections.label: Randstad 2023 quiet quitting survey
sections.summary: A 2023 Randstad survey found 35% of Singaporean workers quiet quit, citing work-life balance, low compensation and lack of career growth.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to a survey conducted in 2023 by HR agency Randstad, 35% of Singaporean workers have engaged in quiet quitting, which is four percentage points higher than the global average.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Among those who have quiet quit, 41% indicated that they did so to improve their work-life balance; 38% attributed it to low compensation and the rising cost of living; and 33% noted a lack of career growth opportunities.

sections.label: Toxic workplaces harm the economy
sections.summary: Toxic workplaces harm individuals and damage the economy through increased turnover, reduced productivity and wasted talents.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Toxic workplaces do not just harm individuals, they damage our entire economy through increased turnover, reduced productivity and wasted talents.

sections.label: Discrimination reporting and independent Statutory Board
sections.summary: MOM's 2023 report shows only 29.5% of discriminated employees sought help, and the speaker urges an independent Statutory Board and internal reporting mechanisms.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to MOM's Fair Employment Practices 2023 report, only 29.5% of employees who experienced discrimination sought help, down from 35.3% in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For this Bill to succeed we need to reverse this trend and I encourage the Ministry to establish an independent Statutory Board with the legislative authority to receive, investigate and report on discrimination complaints by employees in the public, private and community sectors.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the absence of such a body, the Ministry should require all employers to have and actively promote safe and accessible internal mechanisms for employees to report discrimination complaints and to have policies and procedures that guarantee an impartial, confidential, expert and timely investigation of all complaints.

sections.label: Task force to monitor Bill implementation
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a dedicated public, private and community sector task force to monitor the Bill, gather data and recommend adjustments.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To ensure that we keep momentum on this important issue, I would like to suggest that the Ministry establish a dedicated task force comprising relevant members from public, private and community sector to monitor the Bills implementation, gather data on the effectiveness of the Bill, provide regular updates and recommend adjustments based on real world outcomes.

sections.label: Section 10(2) sex definition
sections.summary: Section 10(2) excludes sexual orientation and gender identity from the definition of "sex".

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As many Members have mentioned, specifically, section 10(2) excludes sexual orientation and gender identity from the definition of "sex".

sections.label: LGBTQ workplace discrimination studies
sections.summary: NUS 2024 and AWARE 2022 studies found many LGBTQ respondents experienced workplace discrimination or harassment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A 2024 study by the National University of Singapore (NUS) Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health found that over half of their respondents who were LGBTQ experienced discrimination or harassment at the workplace based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A 2022 study by AWARE and Milieu Insight found that 68% of LGBTQ+ persons reported experiencing discrimination compared to 56% of those who did not identify as LGBTQ.

sections.label: Low reporting of discrimination
sections.summary: Few LGBTQ respondents who faced workplace discrimination reported it to employer, MOM or TAFEP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The NUS School of Public Health survey found that for LGBTQ respondents who experienced workplace discrimination and harassment, only 10.71% reported it to their employer, 0.32% reported it to MOM, and only 0.97%, not even 1%, reported it to TAFEP.

sections.label: Assurance and data request
sections.summary: Member seeks assurance that such discrimination is wrong and asks what data Minister will consider.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Given that the exclusions already exist under the Bill, I hope again that the Minister can provide a clear assurance that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is wrong, regardless of whether this position is codified under legislation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Minister also share what data and factors he will consider in deciding when our laws should expressly prohibit discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity?

sections.label: Support for Bill, outsourced workers
sections.summary: Member supports the Bill, says orientation is unrelated to job ability, but calls it a missed opportunity for outsourced workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Being gay, the last time I thought about it, seemed to have nothing to do with the ability to read a balance book, fix a broken bone, or change a spark plug." Indeed, a person's sexual orientation or gender identity has nothing to do with their ability to do a job well.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I support this Bill which ensures that we can live in a world without discrimination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: And a world that is without discrimination must be inclusive regardless of a person's sexual orientation or gender identity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support the Bill, notwithstanding the points I will be making in this speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am of the view, Sir, that this Bill is a missed opportunity to extend protections to outsourced workers.

sections.label: Gap for outsourced workers
sections.summary: Service buyers are not bound by the Bill, leaving a protection gap for outsourced workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Because this Bill covers employer's responsibilities, service buyers are therefore not subject to the obligations and penalties under this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This presents a gap in the protection regime for outsourced workers because the key determinant of their workplace conditions are actually site owners and not their employers.

sections.label: Obligations on outsourced service buyers
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Minister will eventually extend the Bill's obligations and penalties to buyers of outsourced services, suggesting tripartite guidelines as an immediate step.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: While I raise this, Sir, I am also aware that it is legally complex to place obligations under law on such service buyers and I can understand if the Minister adopts an incremental approach to possibly eventually impose obligations on such service buyers because they are essentially de facto employers and controllers of the workplace fairness of outsourced workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I hope the Minister will consider eventually extending the obligations and penalties under the Bill to buyers of outsourced services.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One way, Sir, that we can immediately deal with this would be to issue tripartite guidelines or amend existing guidelines to specifically proscribe such practices by service buyers.

sections.label: Government's prudent approach to Bill
sections.summary: The Government took time with the Bill because defining and designing an anti-discrimination law is complex and requires a delicate balance to avoid disrupting social harmony.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Leong Mun Wai also asked why the Government took so long with this Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: It is easy to call for a new anti-discrimination law, but it is complex and it is challenging to define and to design a Bill that strikes not just the right balance, I would add, a very fine and delicate balance.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: So, instead of rushing into this, we have approached this in a prudent and a circumspect manner so that we do not disrupt our hard-earned social harmony.

sections.label: Prudent start and TGFEP coverage
sections.summary: With tripartite partners' support, the Government started with a prudent approach reflecting current norms, with the TGFEP covering other workplace discrimination forms.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: With the support of our tripartite partners, we decided to start with a surefooted and a prudent approach, which reflects current societal and workplace norms.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We will complement this Bill with the TGFEP, which will continue to cover other forms of workplace discrimination.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: To Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Saktiandi Supaat's queries, such complaints involve discrimination based on factors, such as physical attributes, medical conditions and criminal records.

sections.label: Guidance on genuine job requirements
sections.summary: The Government agrees it is important to clarify what constitutes a genuine job requirement and will publish further tripartite guidance to support employers' compliance.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We also agree with Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Melvin Yong that it is important to be clear about what constitutes a genuine job requirement to prevent inadvertent discrimination against those with mental health conditions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: We will publish further guidance developed with tripartite partners to support employers' compliance.

sections.label: Job Redesign Grant support
sections.summary: The Government will support employers to implement accommodations, such as through the Job Redesign Grant to defray job redesign and workplace modification costs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: As suggested by Mr Yip Hon Weng, we will support employers to implement such accommodations, like through the Job Redesign Grant to defray the cost of job redesign and workplace modifications.

sections.label: Timing of Tripartite Advisory release
sections.summary: The Government aims to release the Tripartite Advisory around about the same time as the implementation of the legislation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: To Miss Rachel Ong's query, we aim to release the Tripartite Advisory around about the same time with the implementation of legislation.

sections.label: MOM checks on discriminatory employers
sections.summary: Over 600 EP applications from companies were withdrawn or rejected in five years after MOM investigations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: Our robust checks today ensure employers fairly consider all job applicants and we have been rooting out discriminatory employers even before this Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
sentences.text: I have highlighted earlier, before in the past, over 600 EP applications from companies were withdrawn or rejected over the last five years following MOM investigations.

sections.label: WP support for SOGI coverage
sections.summary: WP MPs back Ms He Ting Ru on fair workplace treatment for LGBTQ individuals, covered under TGFEP guidelines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The second point was the Minister raised the example made by my colleague for Sengkang Group Representation Constituency, Ms He Ting Ru, about the call for the legislation to cover individuals of a different sexual orientation and gender identity, what the Minister referred to as SOGI.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I can confirm that all the WP Members of Parliament stand behind our colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, on the point she made.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: LGBTQ individuals deserve to be treated fairly at the workplace.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: That said, I also note even though the coverage is not explicitly included in the Bill, Minister shared that they would be covered under the TGFEP guidelines.

sections.label: SOGI coverage on TAFEP website
sections.summary: The speaker asks that SOGI discrimination coverage under the Tripartite Guidelines be stated explicitly on the TAFEP website.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: But, and it is a big but, this is actually not explicitly stated on the TAFEP website.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: It would mean a lot for the LGBTQ+ community if we can explicitly state on the TAFEP website that discrimination based on SOGI is covered under the Tripartite Guidelines.

sections.label: Listing additional characteristics on website
sections.summary: The speaker says the website should list two additional characteristics and that discrimination will not be tolerated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
sentences.text: TGFEP just sort of leaves them out and, to be inclusive, the website already lists some, it is fair enough that we should list these additional two characteristics.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: I have sort of made it very clear that we will not tolerate any form of discrimination and, today, if we are able to pass the Bill, it is a very significant landmark.

sections.label: Clause 28 retaliation and re-employment
sections.summary: Clause 28 prohibits retaliation against employees raising grievances; other re-employment cases go to the Minister under the Retirement and Re-employment Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Clause 28 prohibits employers from taking any retaliatory action against employees who raise grievances or pursue claims under the Bill, so not offering re-employment is an adverse employment decision, only if it is attributable to retaliation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: In other cases where the employer did not offer re-employment, the affected employee can make representations to the Minister under the Retirement and Re-employment Act.

sections.label: Study on under-employment and PMET ratio
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether MOM studied under-employment and whether the PMET ratio was reviewed after stripping out immigration effects.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, the first thing, the first question —

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, the first question I want to ask is: has the MOM conducted any study on the possibility of under-employment in the Singapore job market?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: By quoting another macro indicator, that is the PMET or PME ratio, he quoted roughly that the ratio has gone up from 50% to 60% over a certain period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But I want to know, has the Government actually looked at this ratio again after stripping out the immigration effect?

sections.label: Foreign-owned firms in Singapore
sections.summary: Foreign-owned firms make up 24% of companies in Singapore and employ about one-third of local residents and over one-third of fresh graduates.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: Foreign-owned firms today account for 24% of all companies in Singapore and they employ about one-third of our local resident workforce and more than one-third of our fresh graduates.

sections.label: Top earners in foreign firms
sections.summary: About 60% of locals in the highest income decile, earning about $13,000 a month and above, work in foreign-owned firms.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: About 60% of locals in the highest income decile, who are earning about approximately $13,000 a month and above, are working in foreign-owned firms.

sections.label: Resident PMET growth 2014-2024
sections.summary: The number of resident PMETs grew faster than EP and S Pass holders between 2014 and 2024.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: The number of resident PMETs has, in fact, grown faster than EP and S Pass holders between 2014 and 2024.

sections.label: Second Bill timeline
sections.summary: With Members' support, the second Bill is envisaged for the second half of this year and implementation by 2026/2027.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: But assuming that we can get all Members' support today, we envisage that the second Bill will come sometime in the second half of this year.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We should get the Bill implemented by 2026/2027.

sections.label: Administrative penalties in subsidiary legislation
sections.summary: The administrative penalties will broadly be prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: So, I am waiting for the explanation to come.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: But broadly, the administrative penalties will be prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

sections.label: Blacklisting as last resort
sections.summary: If they cannot be taken beyond that, they will be blacklisted as a last resort and put up in the public.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: If we are not able to get them beyond that, then obviously, we will blacklist them as a last resort, put it up in the public.

sections.label: Under-employment data with ILO
sections.summary: The government is working with the International Labour Organization on under-employment data and will release results when ready.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: For the record, I hope that this would be the last point.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We are working with the International Labour Organization on the under-employment data.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: When it is ready, we will release the results.
